Anemia with Thrombocytopenia

hemolytic uremic syndrome triad · smear · Coombs test · coagulation studies · its four mimicsAre two cell lines down, is the smear sheared, and are the coagulation studies normal?

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo, bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric · Q — the expected laboratory value; options spanned a decreased platelet count, an increased serum haptoglobin and a positive direct Coombs test
The decision point

Scleral icterus with fatigue is hemolytic anemia, and anuria for 24 hours with pedal edema is acute kidney injury. The third feature of hemolytic uremic syndrome is thrombocytopenia. Shiga toxin damages endothelium, platelets are consumed into microthrombi, and red cells are sheared as they pass. The platelet count falls because of the same process that produces the schistocytes and the bilirubin. The exposure is bloody diarrhea a week ago, in a cluster of people who ate together and recovered.

Defining criteria HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) triad — microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (rising blood urea nitrogen [BUN] and creatinine) · Microangiopathic hemolysis — red cells sheared by platelet microthrombi, giving schistocytes, increased indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin · The preceding illness — Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae; bloody diarrhea first, with HUS appearing about a week later · Coombs in HUS — negative, because the red cells are destroyed mechanically rather than coated by antibody
Pertinent positives & negatives Bloody diarrhea one week ago — Shiga toxin colitis; the one-week latency between the diarrhea and the syndrome is characteristic · Shared meal with relatives who recovered — a point-source exposure that confirms the organism but does not explain the labs; most infected people never develop HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) · Anuria for 24 hours with normal intake, plus 2+ pedal edema — acute kidney injury with volume overload, the renal feature of the triad · Scleral icterus — indirect hyperbilirubinemia from hemolysis, the hemolytic feature of the triad · Fatigue and refusing to get out of bed — symptomatic anemia rather than ongoing volume loss; the diarrhea has resolved · No bruising or petechiae described — consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS is often not severe enough to bleed; its absence never argues against the diagnosis · No fever or neurologic change — the absent neurologic change argues against TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)
Anemia with thrombocytopenia: the differential
ProcessIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hemolytic uremic syndromeChild, Shiga toxin colitis, then endothelial injury with platelet microthrombi ~1 week laterBloody diarrhea → anemia + low platelets + acute kidney injury (AKI), normal coags, negative Coombs(the answer)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpuraUsually adult; ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultralarge von Willebrand multimersNeurologic changes, more common than in HUS; plasma exchange, not supportive careAge 7, no neurologic findings
Disseminated intravascular coagulationA severely ill patient (sepsis, trauma, malignancy); consumption of factors as well as plateletsProlonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with low fibrinogen alongside the schistocytesPT is normal in HUS; no critical illness described
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaIgG coats red cells; lupus, lymphoproliferative disease, or a drugDirect Coombs positive; spherocytes, not schistocytes; platelets and kidneys sparedRenal failure and edema, which antibody-mediated hemolysis does not cause
Isolated thrombocytopenia (immune)Low platelets alone after a viral illness; bruising and petechiae in a well childNormal hemoglobin and a normal smear: one cytopenia, not twoAnemia, jaundice and anuria are all present
Management, in one line HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) is treated supportively with fluid and electrolyte management, transfusion, and dialysis when needed. Withhold antibiotics and antimotility agents in suspected Shiga toxin infection.
Decision spine How many cell lines are down? — Anemia plus a consumed platelet count → the microangiopathy family, not a single-lineage problem · Is the hemolysis mechanical or immune? — Schistocytes with a negative Coombs → mechanical shearing · Are the coagulation studies normal? — Yes → HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) or TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura), not DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) · Which organ, and what came first? — Kidney, after bloody diarrhea in a child → HUS · Marker directions from the mechanism — haptoglobin consumed and falling, reticulocytes rising, indirect bilirubin rising, Coombs negative
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Complete blood count (CBC) with platelets and reticulocytesFirstAnemia with low platelets, reticulocytes highTwo cell lines down with hemolysis: consumption, not marrow failure
Peripheral smearNextSchistocytesMechanical shearing; spherocytes would point to an antibody
Direct Coombs testNextNegativeMechanical destruction; positive means autoimmune hemolysis
PT, aPTT and fibrinogenNextNormalHUS or TTP; prolonged times with low fibrinogen mean DIC
Bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and haptoglobinSupportsIndirect bilirubin and LDH up, haptoglobin lowHemolysis; haptoglobin is consumed binding free hemoglobin
BUN, creatinine and urinalysisConfirmsRising creatinine, little or no urineCompletes the HUS triad after bloody diarrhea; stool Shiga toxin testing names the cause
Bone marrow biopsySkipNot needed once the smear shows schistocytesThe platelets are consumed, not underproduced
Mnemonic TTP pentad (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura): microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, neurologic signs, renal injury. Most patients do not have all five; anemia with schistocytes plus low platelets is enough to act.
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo with bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric; which laboratory value is expected → A decreased platelet count → The third leg of the HUS triad
  2. 5 yo on day 3 of bloody diarrhea, stool culture pending, well hydrated and making urine → Supportive care with fluids, withholding antibiotics → Antibiotics may increase the risk of HUS
  3. 7 yo with hemolytic uremic syndrome, hemoglobin 6.2, urine output 10 mL/h, potassium 6.8 → Hemodialysis → Supportive care includes dialysis
  4. 42 yo F with fever, confusion, schistocytes, platelets 15,000, normal PT and normal creatinine → Plasma exchange → Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
  5. 42 yo F with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, platelets 12,000, no active bleeding → Platelet transfusion → It can worsen TTP; reserve for overt bleeding or an invasive procedure
  6. 60 yo M with gram-negative sepsis, schistocytes, platelets 40,000, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen → Treat the underlying sepsis → Disseminated intravascular coagulation is secondary
  7. 9 yo F with 2 weeks of jaundice and fatigue, spherocytes on smear, direct Coombs positive, normal platelets and creatinine → Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Antibody-coated cells rather than sheared ones
  8. Child with brisk hemolysis; why the serum haptoglobin falls rather than rises → It binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared → Consumed, unlike the acute-phase reactants
  9. 6 yo with bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pale with hemoglobin 8 and platelets 60,000; confirming the mechanism → Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes → Mechanical hemolysis
  10. 5 yo, well appearing, petechiae 2 weeks after a viral illness, platelets 20,000, hemoglobin 12.8, otherwise normal smear → Immune thrombocytopenia → One cytopenia with no hemolysis
Decoy note The cookout and the recovered relatives are epidemiology: they confirm a point-source Shiga toxin exposure but settle no laboratory value. The stool blood "has since resolved"; it stopped days ago and was never chronic, so it does not support iron deficiency. The absence of bruising or petechiae does not argue against a low platelet count. Consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) frequently produces no bleeding at all.
Pearls Bloody diarrhea a week ago plus anuria and jaundice is HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): schistocytes, low platelets, rising creatinine and a negative Coombs test. · Two cytopenias with schistocytes mean mechanical destruction. In mechanical destruction the Coombs test is by definition negative, because no cell is antibody-coated. · Haptoglobin is consumed in hemolysis, while ferritin and other acute-phase reactants rise. A marker falls if the process uses it up and rises if the liver makes more of it. · Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis and fall in marrow failure. A reticulocyte count that fails to rise in a known hemolytic patient is a hematologic emergency. · Normal coagulation studies separate HUS and TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) from DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). Kidney injury after bloody diarrhea in a child points to HUS; brain involvement in an adult points to TTP. · Withhold platelet transfusion in TTP unless there is overt bleeding or an invasive procedure, because it can worsen TTP. Withhold antibiotics in suspected Shiga toxin colitis, because they may increase the risk of HUS.
Pairs with Part II Acute Kidney Injury in a Child covers the acute-kidney-injury compartments and carries the hemolytic uremic syndrome row from the renal side. Part II Hemolytic Anemia covers Coombs-negative hemolysis when the platelets and kidneys are normal. This brief covers the case where both cell lines fall together. Ask: is a second cell line down, and is the smear sheared or spherocytic? Part I Hemolytic Anemia covers hemolysis with a normal platelet count and an antibody rather than a clot. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child starts one step earlier, from the bruise, and sorts it by the platelet count.
Transferable rule For a laboratory abnormality "associated" with a stated mechanism, what matters is the direction each marker moves, not the marker's name. Derive the direction from the mechanism: consumed or produced, mechanical or immune. When the findings form a named syndrome, list its triad rather than re-deriving each component.
Unchecked attributeIncreased serum haptoglobin: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed, so it falls in hemolysis
True-fact-wrong-slotPositive direct Coombs test: Coombs detects antibody-coated cells; HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) destroys red cells mechanically, so the test is negative. Antibody hemolysis would not cause anuria and edema
Salient decoyDecreased ferritin level: The bleeding was acute and has resolved; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and rises with inflammation
Class-vs-memberIncreased PT: DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) also consumes clotting factors and needs a critically ill patient; in HUS the PT is normal
Unchecked attributeDecreased reticulocyte count: Hemolysis is expected to produce reticulocytosis, a rise, as the marrow responds to the anemia

Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant

neonatal respiratory distress causes · bronchopulmonary dysplasiaHow preterm, did labor occur, when did it start, and what does the film show?

WorkupDistress at birthPreterm clockPractice
Bottom line

Time it first. At birth, four facts decide before any pathophysiology: gestational age, whether labor occurred, when distress began and what the film shows; the oxygen response then separates lung from shunt. In the preterm infant each complication has its own window: check the timing before the findings.

  • Transient tachypnea of the newborn: retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs; fluid in the fissures; onset within 2 hours, gone within 24 to 72.
  • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS): preterm surfactant deficiency; distress at birth, ground glass with air bronchograms.
  • Apnea of prematurity: the immature brainstem does not sustain breathing; central pauses, with no obstruction and no lung disease, in an infant well between episodes.
  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD): a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days of life or more; arrested alveolar development, not fibrotic ventilator injury and not air leak.
Workup
Distress at birth
Gestational age, labor, onset, film
DiagnosisSettingThe tell
Transient tachypneaTerm or late preterm; cesarean without labor, macrosomia, maternal diabetes or asthmaFluid in the fissures, perihilar streaking; resolves in 24 to 72 hours
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency, worsening over 48 to 72 hoursLow lung volumes, diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms
Meconium aspirationTerm or post-term, meconium-stained fluid, fetal distressCoarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation
Group B streptococcal pneumoniaRupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxisFilm mimics RDS exactly; temperature instability, neutropenia
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaViscera crush the developing lungScaphoid abdomen, shifted heart sounds; bowel loops in the chest with a displaced heart
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missFailed transition, often after asphyxia or aspirationPre- to postductal gap above 10%, poorly oxygen-responsive
PolycythemiaIntrauterine hypoxia or placental transfusionPlethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film; venous hematocrit above 65% in a term neonate
Exit ramps Diaphragmatic hernia – never bag-mask (it inflates bowel inside the chest): intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma), decompress with a nasogastric tube; the lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists · Displaced heart sounds – scaphoid abdomen with absent breath sounds on the defect side: hernia; distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant: tension pneumothorax, needle decompression; well, heart on the right, no distress: dextrocardia · Diabetic mother – raises the risk of transient tachypnea and delays surfactant maturation, so RDS can appear at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe
The preterm clock
Apnea of prematurity Definition – a pause over 20 seconds, or a shorter one with bradycardia or desaturation · Diagnosis – clinical, after the mimics are checked: anemia, infection and intraventricular hemorrhage, plus glucose and electrolytes (seizure and reflux are the other usual mimics) · Versus hemorrhage – lethargy, a tense fontanelle, a growing head or seizures; cranial ultrasound · Management – caffeine, a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia Severity – graded by support required at 36 weeks postmenstrual age · Prevention – surfactant and gentler ventilation turned it from fibrotic injury into developmental arrest; caffeine and vitamin A each reduce it · Management – supportive: oxygen, nutrition, fluid restriction; alveoli keep forming over months · Complications – pulmonary hypertension, systemic hypertension, recurrent respiratory infections, neurodevelopmental delay · Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – first season, under 8 months: nirsevimab or clesrovimab; second season, 8 to 19 months: nirsevimab only, for BPD that needed oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids in the 6 months before the season; palivizumab is no longer available after December 31, 2025 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance)
Practice
  1. 1-hour-old boy born at 40 weeks by cesarean without labor is tachypneic chest x-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures Afebrile · birth weight 4200 g · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 88% on room air, 98% on oxygen → Transient tachypnea of the newborn → retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs: fluid in the fissures appears in no competing diagnosis, and saturation correcting from 88% to 98% on oxygen is alveolar fluid, not a shunt. Cesarean without labor misses the catecholamine surge that switches the epithelium to absorbing fluid; macrosomia adds risk. Respiratory distress syndrome is the right category but a preterm member, and group B streptococcal pneumonia needs risk factors the stem never supplies. Supportive care: onset within 2 hours, and it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so an infant breathing normally by 48 hours fits
  2. 6-week-old boy born at 26 weeks still needs supplemental oxygen on nasal cannula oxygen every day since birth enteral feeds introduced today Weight gain appropriate on total parenteral nutrition Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on 0.5 L/min → Arrested alveolar development → a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days or more has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and since surfactant and gentler ventilation it is arrested alveolar development: fewer alveoli, less septation, disrupted vasculogenesis. Fibrotic ventilator injury is the old form, and air leak belongs to the first days on high pressures, weeks before this. Feeds introduced today suggest refeeding syndrome, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition
  3. 6-hour-old girl born at term has tachypnea and grunting membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery maternal fever 38.5 °C in labor; no intrapartum prophylaxis Temperature unstable since birth T 35.9 °C · HR 176/min · respiratory rate 74/min → Blood culture and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever and no intrapartum prophylaxis, with temperature instability, is early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis. Its film mimics respiratory distress syndrome exactly, so surfactant misses it, and observing without antibiotics leaves the infection untreated: culture and start ampicillin and gentamicin
  4. Term newborn boy has severe respiratory distress at delivery scaphoid abdomen heart sounds displaced to the right chest x-ray shows bowel gas in the left hemithorax T 36.6 °C · HR 92/min · oxygen saturation 64% → Intubate with limited peak pressures and decompress the stomach → a scaphoid abdomen with displaced heart sounds and bowel in the chest is a diaphragmatic hernia. Bag-mask ventilation inflates bowel inside the chest, so intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma) and decompress with a nasogastric tube. Needle decompression is for a tension pneumothorax: a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant
  5. 4-day-old boy born at 29 weeks in neonatal intensive care several 20-second breathing pauses today, bradycardia and desaturation ends with stimulation; pink, active, feeding well between Cultures negative; antibiotics stopped T 36.9 °C, stable · glucose, electrolytes, hemoglobin, ultrasound normal → Begin caffeine → a central pause from an immature brainstem, starting on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between spells, with the mimics checked (infection, anemia, intraventricular hemorrhage, glucose, electrolytes), is apnea of prematurity. Caffeine is a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue. Antibiotics answer the infant who is ill between spells; dexamethasone and albuterol are used for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, not for apnea
  6. 2-hour-old boy born at 29 weeks is grunting and retracting chest x-ray shows low lung volumes diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms Membranes ruptured at delivery T 36.8 °C · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 86% on room air → Respiratory distress syndrome → surfactant deficiency in a preterm infant (under 34 weeks) gives distress at birth, worsening over 48 to 72 hours, with low volumes, ground glass and air bronchograms: give surfactant and CPAP. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures in a term infant; group B streptococcal pneumonia mimics this film exactly but needs risk factors (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) this stem does not supply
  7. 2-day-old boy born at term is plethoric, lethargic and feeding poorly venous hematocrit 72% no better after 12 hours of intravenous fluids Born after delayed cord clamping Afebrile · glucose 48 mg/dL · HR 156/min → Partial exchange transfusion → most polycythemic infants are ruddy and asymptomatic; hyperviscosity brings lethargy, irritability and jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, respiratory distress, poor feeding and cyanosis. Hydration by feeds or glucose-containing intravenous fluids comes first; symptomatic hyperviscosity despite it needs a partial exchange transfusion, which swaps blood for saline to lower viscosity. A double-volume exchange replaces the infant's blood with donor red cells and is used for severe hyperbilirubinemia, and furosemide adds fluid loss, which can make the blood even thicker; true dehydration is rare in the first 2 days, while the neonate still carries excess extracellular fluid
  8. 8-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks is cyanotic preductal saturation 88%, postductal 76% minimal improvement on 100% oxygen chest x-ray nearly clear Delivered through meconium-stained fluid Afebrile · HR 168/min · BP 62/38 mm Hg → Obtain an echocardiogram → a pre- to postductal gap above 10% that barely responds to oxygen is right-to-left ductal shunting: persistent pulmonary hypertension, a failed transition often after asphyxia or aspiration. Echocardiography shows high pulmonary pressure in a structurally normal heart and excludes cyanotic heart disease. Surfactant treats alveolar disease, which corrects on oxygen, and reassurance misses a can't-miss diagnosis
  9. 12-day-old girl born at 26 weeks has abdominal distension bloody stools on day 10 of enteral feeds abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis T 35.9 °C · HR 182/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Necrotizing enterocolitis → a preterm infant on enteral feeds with distension, bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis has bacterial invasion of the bowel wall: keep nil by mouth, give intravenous antibiotics and consult surgery. Allergic proctocolitis is the well infant with bloody stool; pneumatosis intestinalis is the tell that names this can't-miss diagnosis over it and over malrotation with volvulus
  10. 1-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks by cesarean without labor is breathing fast chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures with perihilar streaking Mother asks to breastfeed now Afebrile · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 93% on oxygen → Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen → neonatal tachypnea is a respiratory rate above 60 per minute, and feeding at a rate of 80 risks aspiration: keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and oxygen. Intubation and surfactant are for the preterm surfactant-deficient lung, not retained fluid in a term infant
  11. 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, is in preterm labor at 29 weeks cervix dilated 5 cm delivery expected within 48 hours T 37.0 °C · BP 118/72 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 140/min → Antenatal betamethasone → antenatal betamethasone gives the fetal lung the cortisol signal that drives surfactant maturation (the signal fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes); corticosteroid exposure before delivery lowers rates of respiratory distress syndrome, intracranial hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis and death, while surfactant can only be given after birth; tocolysis buys time for the steroid course and has not been shown to improve neonatal outcomes on its own
  12. 1-hour-old boy born at 37 weeks has grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled diabetes chest x-ray shows diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms Afebrile · birth weight 4300 g · oxygen saturation 85% on room air → Fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol, delaying surfactant maturation → fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol and suppresses phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol production, delaying surfactant maturation; the pneumocytes are not directly injured, and placental vessel disease from diabetic vascular complications can give a small-for-gestational-age infant, not a 4300 g one
  13. 5-day-old girl born at 30 weeks has new apnea and bradycardia since this morning lethargic and mottled between episodes abdominal distension and feeding intolerance No antibiotics so far T 35.8 °C, unstable · HR 188/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Blood culture and empiric antibiotics → an infant who is ill between spells (temperature instability, feeding intolerance or poor perfusion) has suspected sepsis, not simple apnea of prematurity: culture and treat. Caffeine is for the infant well between spells; anemia of prematurity comes weeks later, pale with a low hemoglobin; this tachycardia is sepsis
  14. 2-day-old girl was diagnosed with a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia at birth intubated; saturations now falling echocardiogram shows suprasystemic pulmonary pressures right hand saturation 92% · foot saturation 78% · HR 170/min → Inhaled nitric oxide → a hand-foot gap above 10% is right-to-left ductal shunting from pulmonary hypertension of the hypoplastic lung. Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) is the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but this cyanosis is not a closing duct; a chest tube treats a pneumothorax, not shunting. The lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists; the gap itself shows the duct is already open, so the target is pulmonary vasodilation
  15. 3-day-old boy born at 27 weeks has abrupt hypoxia on high-pressure mechanical ventilation since birth chest x-ray shows unilateral perivascular cystic lucencies No distended, hyperresonant hemithorax Afebrile · HR 172/min · oxygen saturation 78% → Pulmonary interstitial emphysema → air dissects into the interstitium on high ventilator pressures in the first days: cystic lucencies and abrupt decompensation; reduce ventilator pressures. Tension pneumothorax gives a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax needing needle decompression, and respiratory distress syndrome, though it worsens over 48 to 72 hours, shows ground glass with air bronchograms
  16. 10-hour-old girl born at 29 weeks has needed CPAP since birth rising oxygen requirement, now 60% worsening retractions chest x-ray shows ground glass with air bronchograms T 36.8 °C · oxygen saturation 86% on CPAP → Intubate and give surfactant → worsening surfactant deficiency despite CPAP means CPAP has failed: intubate and give surfactant. Closer observation leaves the failure untreated, and antibiotics alone do not replace surfactant
  17. 6-hour-old boy born at term is ruddy and jittery breathing fast with no retractions chest x-ray is clear; no hepatomegaly; normal heart sounds Mother had preeclampsia Afebrile · glucose 32 mg/dL · respiratory rate 70/min · HR 150/min → Polycythemia → plethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film is polycythemia. Intrauterine hypoxia drives erythropoietin (preeclampsia, maternal diabetes or hypertension, smoking, growth restriction), or placental transfusion adds blood (delayed cord clamping, twin-twin transfusion); hyperviscosity brings jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea; check a venous hematocrit (above 65%). Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, glycogen storage disease type I brings hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis, and cyanotic heart disease is excluded by a normal heart and exam
  18. 14-month-old boy born at 30 weeks is seen at a well visit has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, on diuretics until 3 months ago his second RSV season starts next month Afebrile · respiratory rate 36/min · oxygen saturation 96% on room air → Nirsevimab prophylaxis → chronic lung disease of prematurity that needed medical support (supplemental oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids) in the 6 months before the second season qualifies for a second-season dose, and nirsevimab is the product recommended; palivizumab is no longer available from December 31, 2025, and the prophylaxis is an antibody, not an infant vaccine
  19. Term newborn girl has severe cyanosis at 12 hours no improvement on 100% oxygen no retractions; comfortable tachypnea chest radiograph structurally normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 68% on 100% oxygen · HR 160/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → cyanosis that does not correct on oxygen in a comfortable infant with a normal film is a shunt (the hyperoxia test, still keyed on exams though largely abandoned clinically): suspect cyanotic congenital heart disease and start prostaglandin E1 pending echocardiography. Surfactant treats alveolar disease that corrects on oxygen; inhaled nitric oxide treats pulmonary hypertension, whose tell is a ductal saturation gap above 10%
  20. 3-week-old boy born at 28 weeks is given caffeine for central apneic spells well between spells His parents ask when the spells should stop Afebrile · HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% on room air → By about his expected due date → the brainstem breathing center matures by term corrected age, so spells resolve by about the expected due date; 28 days is the bronchopulmonary dysplasia clock, not the apnea clock
  21. 1-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks has tachypnea and retractions delivered through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress chest x-ray shows coarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation Afebrile · respiratory rate 84/min · oxygen saturation 87% → Meconium aspiration syndrome → term or post-term delivery through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress, with coarse patchy asymmetric infiltrates and hyperinflation; watch for pneumothorax and pulmonary hypertension. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, and for congenital pneumonia nothing in this stem points to infection (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis)
  22. 2-hour-old girl born at 36 weeks has central cyanosis, grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes chest x-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacities Afebrile · saturation 64% rising to 82% on oxygen · pre- and postductal readings equal → Surfactant → maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturation, so an infant of a diabetic mother can develop respiratory distress syndrome at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe. Ground glass with equal pre- and postductal readings and a partial oxygen response is lung disease, not a ductal shunt, so prostaglandin E1 is not the answer; steroids for the lung are the antenatal betamethasone given before delivery
  23. 4-month-old boy born at 28 weeks has poor weight gain needed supplemental oxygen until 3 months of age loud P2 liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · respiratory rate 56/min · oxygen saturation 93% on room air → Pulmonary artery hypertension → pulmonary hypertension is a complication of bronchopulmonary dysplasia that arrives months later, with a loud P2 and poor growth: obtain an echocardiogram. Systemic hypertension and recurrent respiratory infections are also complications, but a loud P2 is the pulmonic sound, and aspiration is a trigger to screen for in this pulmonary hypertension, not the diagnosis; the enlarged liver can reflect right heart failure
  24. 4-day-old girl born at term was diagnosed with transient tachypnea on day 1 still breathing fast at 96 hours of life Feeding by nasogastric tube Afebrile · respiratory rate 74/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air → Re-evaluate for another diagnosis → transient is a diagnostic criterion, not a description: it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so tachypnea beyond 72 hours means the diagnosis was wrong; look again. Continued observation and discharge both keep the wrong label
Common wrong answers Refeeding syndrome: feeds introduced today suggest it, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition. Pulmonary interstitial emphysema at 28 days: real ventilator pathology, but it belongs to the first days. RDS in a term infant: the right category, a preterm member. Group B streptococcal pneumonia: needs risk factors the stem must supply. Prostaglandin in a diaphragmatic hernia: the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but the cyanosis comes from hypoplastic lungs and pulmonary hypertension, not a closing duct. Diaphragmatic hernia at an hour with fissural fluid: it presents at delivery with a scaphoid abdomen.
Pairs with Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant: the well infant with bloody stool; here, the ill preterm infant. Ask: is the infant preterm, distended and unwell? Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant: intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia of prematurity, the mimics to exclude before calling a spell apnea of prematurity. Ask: is the infant well between episodes? Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the same distress in the first hours. Ask: is this fluid in normal lungs, or lungs that never developed? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the step before, where work of breathing, the oxygen response and the limb gradient sort lung from heart. Part I Hypoxemia: the physiology under the oxygen response.
Transferable rule

Match the clock before the findings. Birth: RDS or transient tachypnea, sorted by gestational age, labor, onset and the film. Ventilator days: air leak. Day 2 to 3 spells in a well infant: apnea of prematurity. Oxygen at 28 days: BPD. Months: pulmonary hypertension. When the history states a diagnostic criterion exactly, make that diagnosis directly.

Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome

glomerular or not, then symptomatic or not · nephritis weeks after strep: complement and volumeIs it glomerular, how long since the infection, is complement low, and is the child overloaded?

Glomerular or notNephritic syndromePractice
Bottom line

With dysuria, leukocyte esterase and pyuria, the blood is part of the cystitis, not a separate workup. Otherwise ask in order: is it glomerular, and if not, does a symptom name the cause?

  • Glomerular hematuria: any of brown, tea or cola urine, red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, protein, edema or hypertension; check creatinine, complement levels and a complete blood count (CBC).
  • Non-glomerular hematuria: bright red urine or clots, normal red cell shape, no protein. With no symptom to name the cause: renal and bladder ultrasound, the first image for painless gross hematuria, since a young child's kidney stone is often painless; urine culture; and urine calcium/creatinine ratio, high in asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross.
  • Nephritic syndrome: hematuria with red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, hypertension, edema, oliguria and a rising creatinine; protein present but usually below the nephrotic range.
  • Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN): about 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis and up to about 6 weeks after impetigo. Hematuria during or within days of an upper respiratory infection is immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy.
  • Complement clock: C3 (complement component 3) low at onset, back to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks; still low after 8 weeks suggests a different lesion.
Glomerular or not
Glomerular vs non-glomerular hematuria
GlomerularNon-glomerular

Nephritic syndrome after strep
Acute nephritis in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness script and tellAgainst it 2 weeks after a sore throat
PSGNImmune complexes after group A strep pharyngitis or impetigo; edema, hypertension, cola urine; weeks later, low C3, normal by 6 to 8 weeks; positive ASO or anti-DNase B; children recover over weeksThe answer
IgA nephropathyMesangial IgA; recurrent gross hematuria in an older child or young adult, during or within days of an infection; normal C3Two-week gap; edema and hypertension, not isolated episodes
IgA vasculitis nephritisSmall-vessel IgA vasculitis; kidney disease can follow the rash by weeks; palpable purpura on legs and buttocks, arthritis, abdominal pain; normal C3No rash, joint or abdominal pain
Lupus nephritis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)Immune-complex nephritis that does not resolve; lupus mostly in adolescent girls; persistently low complement; lupus lowers C3 and C4 (complement component 4), with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA)Decided at 8 weeks: an unrecovered C3 calls for further investigation, including a biopsy

Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy has bright red urine since yesterday No dysuria, trauma or recent infection no edema or flank tenderness BP 100/65 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts; leukocyte esterase and nitrite negative → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → bright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension is nonglomerular, and no symptom names a cause. In a young child a kidney stone is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone; the ultrasound finds many stones and any obstruction with no radiation and also excludes a renal mass such as Wilms tumor. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Noncontrast CT is more sensitive for small stones but carries radiation, so in a child it follows a nondiagnostic ultrasound
  2. 8-year-old boy has 2 days of tea-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago, resolved without treatment puffy eyelids; mild pretibial edema urine: red cell casts, 2+ protein BP 140/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → a latent period of weeks, not days, with red cell casts, protein and hypertension: expect a low C3 that normalizes by 6 to 8 weeks and a positive ASO or anti-DNase B. IgA nephropathy bleeds during or within days of an upper respiratory infection with a normal C3. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is the nephritis that does not resolve, with a persistently low complement; it is raised when the C3 is still low at 8 weeks
  3. 8-year-old girl was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis yesterday periorbital and pedal edema Her physician considers drugs for her blood pressure BP 150/96 mm Hg · creatinine 1.7 mg/dL · potassium 6.0 mEq/L → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors raise potassium and can lower the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in AKI, and this potassium is already high. Furosemide treats the overload that drives the edema and pressure, and nifedipine follows if pressure stays high after diuresis
  4. 14-year-old boy receiving cyclophosphamide has 2 days of bright red urine with clots suprapubic discomfort; no flank pain Urine culture shows no growth Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · urine: protein negative, no casts → Hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein → bright red urine with clots on cyclophosphamide is a hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein: give mesna and hydration. After a transplant, think of BK (a polyomavirus) or adenovirus. A bacterial cystitis needs significant bacteriuria on culture, and bladder cancer is very rare in children
  5. 7-year-old girl has microscopic hematuria on two routine urinalyses Well, with no dysuria, flank pain or edema urine: no protein, no casts, normal red cell shape BP 98/60 mm Hg · urine culture negative · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL → Urine calcium/creatinine ratio → hypercalciuria is the most common cause of asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross, in a well child and the main risk factor for a stone; a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio finds it. A biopsy is a glomerular test, and this urine has no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, very rare in children
  6. 16-year-old boy has a third episode of cola-colored urine each began 1 to 2 days into a sore throat Between episodes he feels well urine: red cells, 1+ protein BP 118/74 mm Hg · C3 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → IgA nephropathy → synpharyngitic hematuria, within 1 to 2 days of the sore throat, recurrent, with a normal C3: mesangial IgA, typical in an older child or young adult. Poststreptococcal disease comes weeks after the infection with a low C3. Thin basement membrane disease usually presents as isolated microscopic hematuria; gross bleeds occur in only a minority, often after infection
  7. 9-year-old boy has headache, lethargy and 2 days of low urine output Sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital, scrotal and pedal edema; no rash BP 170/102 mm Hg, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, normal blood count · urine: moderate blood, 2+ protein → Furosemide → hematuria with protein, hypertension, edema and a rising creatinine two weeks after a sore throat is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water, and the edema and hypertension both come from that volume: the first drug is a loop diuretic, with sodium and fluid restriction. Saline answers the low urine output and raised creatinine, but this child is overloaded, not dry. Plasmapheresis treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease; this disease is immune-complex and self-limited. Headache and lethargy at this pressure are signs of hypertensive encephalopathy, so a calcium channel blocker is added alongside the diuretic now rather than after diuresis; it is not among these options
  8. 68-year-old man has two episodes of painless bright red urine Smokes one pack daily for 45 years no dysuria or flank pain Afebrile · BP 136/84 mm Hg · urine: over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein, casts or leukocyte esterase → Cystoscopy + CT urography → painless gross hematuria in an older adult or smoker earns CT urography and cystoscopy, which find a mass or stone; bladder cancer is the concern at this age. A repeat urinalysis in weeks delays that, and a renal ultrasound alone skips the cystoscopy and detects far fewer upper tract urothelial tumors than CT urography
  9. 10-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 3 months ago Seen at a scheduled follow-up visit edema has resolved microscopic hematuria persists on urinalysis BP 108/68 mm Hg · C3 still low · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL → Renal biopsy → a C3 that has not recovered by 8 weeks calls for further investigation, including a biopsy, to look for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis. Microscopic hematuria may persist for up to 5 years, but C3 returns to normal within 6 to 8 weeks in about 80%; waiting 3 more months delays the biopsy, and a repeat ASO shows only recent strep infection, not why the C3 stays low
  10. 8-year-old boy has had 3 days of tea-colored urine He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital edema urine: red cell casts, 1+ protein Afebrile · BP 138/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Serum C3 level → nephritis weeks after pharyngitis: a low C3 with a normal or mildly low C4 supports it; a normal C3 means IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis, and a low C3 and C4 suggest lupus. A biopsy is generally only for an atypical course (C3 still low after 8 weeks or worsening), and an ultrasound shows size and structure, not immune complexes
  11. 10-year-old boy has microscopic hematuria on every urinalysis since age 4 sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry His maternal uncle had kidney failure at 30 BP 112/70 mm Hg · urine: 1+ protein · C3 normal → Alport syndrome → persistent hematuria with sensorineural hearing loss and a family history of kidney failure is a type IV collagen defect, usually X-linked, progressing slowly to kidney failure. Thin basement membrane disease does not bring deafness. IgA nephropathy bleeds in recurrent gross episodes during or within days of an upper respiratory infection
  12. 11-year-old boy fell onto bicycle handlebars 3 hours ago left flank pain, bruising; bright red urine alert; abdomen soft, left flank tender HR 96/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · large blood, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts → Contrast CT of the abdomen → hematuria after abdominal or flank trauma: CT shows and stages the renal injury. Ultrasound may be used in children, but CT is preferred, and waiting a week to repeat the urinalysis leaves the injury unstaged
  13. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 2 days ago headache After 24 hours of furosemide with sodium and fluid restriction alert, no respiratory distress BP 165/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.8 mEq/L → Add nifedipine → pressure that stays high after 24 hours of diuresis is the indication for a calcium channel blocker, so waiting another day is not the step. Watch for hypertensive encephalopathy: headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures. Dialysis is for refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia, none of which is present
  14. 17-year-old girl has 5 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner; no fever or flank pain urine: leukocyte esterase positive, 20 white cells/hpf, a few red cells urine culture: no growth Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT → sterile pyuria with dysuria in a sexually active adolescent: test for chlamydia and gonorrhea with a nucleic acid amplification test. Other causes of sterile pyuria are renal tuberculosis, interstitial nephritis, a partially treated urinary tract infection and appendicitis. A culture for bacterial cystitis already grew nothing, which is what makes this pyuria sterile, and a renal ultrasound answers flank pain with crystals or painless gross hematuria
  15. 6-year-old girl has cola-colored urine and puffy eyelids Crusted sores on her legs 4 weeks ago red cell casts; no rash or joint pain BP 138/90 mm Hg · C3 low · C4 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → nephritis up to about 6 weeks after impetigo with a low C3 and normal C4, expected to normalize within 8 weeks; anti-DNase B is the better strep marker after impetigo. IgA nephropathy bleeds within days of an infection with a normal C3, and IgA vasculitis brings palpable purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain with a normal C3
  16. 9-year-old girl has 2 days of brown urine puffy eyelids each morning mild pretibial edema BP 132/86 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, protein 2+, red cell casts · no leukocyte esterase or nitrite → Serum creatinine, complement levels and CBC → brown urine with protein, casts, edema and hypertension is glomerular hematuria: check creatinine, complement levels and a CBC. A low C3 after a recent strep infection points to postinfectious glomerulonephritis. The ultrasound and calcium/creatinine ratio belong to the nonglomerular branch
How NBME framed it: question 1

8-year-old girl with 6 days of intermittent headache, tiredness and little appetite, then 2 days of brown urine Vomited yesterday morning; no abdominal pain, diarrhea or dysuria Sore throat and fever 2 weeks ago that cleared without treatment; previously healthy, no medications; normal growth and development mildly pale, not distressed; height 50th percentile, weight 75th T 36.7 °C · HR 108/min · respiratory rate 16/min · BP 138/88 mm Hg large, mildly red tonsils without exudate; lungs clear grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, no rub or gallop; abdomen normal; warm extremities with 1+ edema serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL · urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL · sodium 132 mEq/L · potassium 5.2 mEq/L · chloride 100 mEq/L · bicarbonate 15 mEq/L urine: blood 2+ · protein 1+ · red cell casts too numerous to count · pH 5 · specific gravity 1.020 · Gram stain: no organisms

Most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Antinuclear antibody assay: pulls toward lupus nephritis; but it is neither sensitive nor specific here, and lupus lowers both C3 and C4.
  • Urine culture: the urine is abnormal; but a culture answers a urinary tract infection; there is no dysuria and the Gram stain shows no organisms.
  • Renal ultrasonography: the creatinine is rising; but immune-complex deposits are microscopic, not visible on ultrasound.

Down to two: serum C3 or echocardiography. Serum C3: brown urine with casts, protein, hypertension and edema 2 weeks after a sore throat; deposited immune complexes consume C3, so the serum level falls. The soft ejection murmur after the sore throat baits rheumatic carditis, but the lungs are clear, so heart failure is unlikely.

Management ladder for PSGN Volume overload – inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water; edema and hypertension both come from that volume; headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures mean hypertensive encephalopathy · Every child – supportive care with sodium and fluid restriction · Loop diuretic – furosemide first, for edema or hypertension from volume overload; saline for the oliguria would worsen it · Calcium channel blocker – nifedipine when pressure stays high after diuresis or encephalopathy appears; ACE inhibitors only with caution in AKI because of hyperkalemia · Dialysis – refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia · No role – plasmapheresis, since the disease is self-limited · Antibiotics – treat a still-active strep infection but do not change the renal course
Nitrite is only about 50% sensitive It needs a nitrate-reducing organism (Enterococcus, S. saprophyticus and Pseudomonas are not) and adequate bladder dwell time. A negative nitrite never excludes a urinary tract infection when leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms agree.
Painless gross hematuria in a child A kidney stone in a young child is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone, and crystals are not always seen. Hypercalciuria is the main risk factor: look for earlier microscopic hematuria and a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio. The renal and bladder ultrasound comes first; noncontrast CT only if it is nondiagnostic. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Meatal irritation is painful and visible on exam: reassure.
Course Nephritis days after an upper respiratory infection is IgA nephropathy; weeks after pharyngitis or impetigo, PSGN. Treating strep pharyngitis promptly prevents rheumatic fever but does not reliably prevent PSGN. Children usually recover fully within weeks, although microscopic hematuria may persist for up to 5 years; adults are more likely to develop chronic kidney disease.
Common wrong answers A negative nitrite overruling leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms. Cystoscopy in a child: right for an older adult, but bladder cancer is very rare in a 6-year-old, so the ultrasound comes first. Noncontrast CT before the ultrasound: more sensitive for small stones, but radiation. A 24-hour urine protein or kidney biopsy for bright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Normal saline for a low urine output in an overloaded child. Plasmapheresis: treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; PSGN is immune-complex and self-limited. Lisinopril first: risks hyperkalemia in AKI; diuresis first, then a calcium channel blocker. Protein restriction: for chronic kidney disease, not a self-limited acute nephritis.
Pairs with Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child: protein without red cells, with normal pressure and creatinine; there a normotensive 3-year-old with periorbital edema is treated on presentation rather than biopsied. Ask: does the urine show red cells and casts, or protein alone? Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes starts one step earlier: is the swelling local to the eye? Part I Acute Kidney Injury in a Child: the AKI that does need fluids. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child sends the renal involvement of IgA vasculitis here. Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia: HUS. Part II Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child: protein on a routine dipstick in a child with no symptoms.
Transferable rule

With a full lab panel, base the diagnosis on the pattern of the panel, not the most alarming single value; a discordant component reflects a test's limited sensitivity and does not overrule the pattern. In a child with AKI, decide whether the kidney needs volume given or removed before choosing a drug: edema with hypertension means overload, so the loop diuretic comes first and saline is harmful.

Constipation in a Child

withholding cycle · alarm signs · impacted or not · oral laxative before any rectal treatment · maintenance for monthsIs growth normal and the examination benign, and is there stool in the rectum?

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo M, hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, nontender abdomen, anal fissure · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned an oral osmotic laxative, a rectal enema and abdominal radiography
The decision point

Stools were daily and soft until toilet training began, and the pain came before the hardness worsened. This is the withholding cycle: a painful stool leads the child to hold, the rectum desiccates the retained stool, and the next stool hurts more. The anal fissure results from the cycle and worsens it. Growth on the 75th percentile, a nontender abdomen and a normal perineum mean no alarm signs, so treat rather than investigate. Give an oral osmotic laxative to make the next stool painless.

Defining criteria Alarm signs — delayed passage of meconium, fever or vomiting, ribbon stools, poor growth, severe abdominal distension, and abnormal examination findings such as a displaced anus or a tuft at the gluteal cleft · Cow's-milk limit — 16 to 24 oz per day at ages 2 to 5 years; this child's 24 oz is at the limit, not above it · Complications that are not alarm signs — anal fissure, hemorrhoids, enuresis and urinary tract infections; each argues for the functional diagnosis rather than against it
Pertinent positives & negatives Onset coincides with toilet training — the commonest trigger, with solid-food and cow's-milk introduction and school entry; points to a behavioral rather than anatomic cause · Previously daily soft stools — normal baseline function excludes a congenital motility defect, which would have presented earlier · Cries and screams with defecation — pain drives withholding and is what the laxative treats · Growth tracking at the 75th percentile — no growth alarm sign; effectively excludes Hirschsprung disease, hypothyroidism and celiac disease · Anal fissure — a complication of hard stools and the reason to avoid a rectal enema · Abdomen firm and mildly distended but nontender — stool load without obstruction; severe distension or tenderness would be an alarm sign · 24 oz of milk, refuses fruit — diet contributes and should be modified, not eliminated · Urinates in the toilet without difficulty — normal bladder function argues against a neurologic cause

Numbers that gate & exit ramps Delayed meconium with ribbon stools and poor growth → Hirschsprung disease, contrast enema or manometry, then rectal suction biopsy · sacral dimple, hair tuft or a displaced anus → spinal imaging for occult dysraphism · vomiting or severe distension with pain → abdominal x-ray, because severe impaction mimics obstruction · overflow soiling in an older child → impaction with encopresis, so disimpact before maintenance and tell the parents the soiling is not deliberate · milk intake well above 24 oz with pallor → reduce milk and check for iron deficiency.

Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M with hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, a nontender abdomen and an anal fissure → Initiate an oral osmotic laxative → Functional constipation
  2. 6 yo M with involuntary soiling of his underwear and a palpable suprapubic stool mass, without an anal fissure → Disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapy → Impaction with overflow incontinence
  3. 4 yo F with fecal impaction requiring disimpaction who has a painful anal fissure on examination → High-dose oral polyethylene glycol → Enemas cause further rectal trauma
  4. 2 yo M with constipation and pallor who drinks 40 oz of cow's milk daily and eats little else → Reduce cow's milk intake and start a laxative → Milk volume above the recommended limit
  5. 3 yo F with constipation, daytime urinary incontinence and a tuft of hair over the sacrum → Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine → Occult spinal dysraphism
  6. 5 yo M whose constipation persists after 3 months of adequate laxative and dietary therapy, with normal growth and examination → Anorectal manometry → Refractory to standard therapy
  7. Newborn who first passed meconium at 60 hours, now with ribbon-like stools, abdominal distension and poor weight gain → Hirschsprung disease → Contrast enema or manometry, then rectal suction biopsy
  8. 8-month-old with constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia and a large anterior fontanelle → Congenital hypothyroidism → Check the TSH
  9. Why one painful bowel movement can produce weeks of worsening constipation in a toddler → Withholding desiccates stool in the rectum→ so the next defecation hurts more, which reinforces withholding; The cycle is the disease
  10. 3 yo M with functional constipation who drinks 24 oz of cow's milk daily; which management is inappropriate → Discontinuing cow's milk entirely → Guidance describes only a time-limited trial off cow's-milk protein (2 to 4 weeks in intractable constipation), not permanent withdrawal
  11. 15-month-old with constipation since infancy refractory to dietary changes, thin caliber stools, distended abdomen, explosive stool and gas on rectal exam → Contrast enema → Hirschsprung disease
Decoy note Refusing to eat fruit and the milk volume suggest a dietary cause, but the milk is at the limit, not above it, so diet is a contributor to adjust. Finding a firm, mildly distended abdomen is not an alarm sign; the alarm signs are severe distension and tenderness, and neither is present. The anal fissure is an expected complication of functional constipation, not evidence of another diagnosis; its only effect on management is to rule out the rectal route.
Pearls A growing child with painful hard stools and a normal examination gets an oral osmotic laxative, not a rectal procedure or imaging. · Childhood constipation is a behavioral cycle with a mechanical consequence. The laxative makes stools painless so the child stops withholding; continue it for at least 2 months. · The three common triggers are solid food and cow's milk, toilet training, and school entry; onset at one of them supports the diagnosis. · An anal fissure is a complication of constipation, not a competing diagnosis, and is the reason to disimpact by mouth rather than by rectum. · Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and poor growth, and fissures are uncommon in it; normal growth with a fissure indicates functional disease. · Growth is the most informative alarm sign; a child tracking a percentile has essentially excluded hypothyroidism, celiac disease and Hirschsprung disease. · Enuresis and urinary tract infections are complications of constipation, so in a child with both, treat the bowel first.
Pairs with Part II Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult is the adult counterpart of tier 2: there the rectal vault is full and an enema is first-line; here the vault is not full and the fissure rules out the rectal route. Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers infants, and Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the dysraphism the perineal examination screens for. Ask: is growth normal, and is there stool in the rectum?
Transferable rule With no alarm signs and a normal examination, treat; investigate only when an alarm sign is present. A complication of the diagnosis supports it but can still change management, as an anal fissure rules out the rectal route.
Unchecked attributeDiscontinue milk: 24 oz is within the recommended 16 to 24 oz range; guidance describes only a time-limited trial off cow's-milk protein (2 to 4 weeks in intractable constipation), not permanent withdrawal
Sequencing trapObtain abdominal radiograph: The film is for severe impaction that mimics obstruction, with pain and vomiting; this abdomen is nontender and benign
Salient decoyAdminister rectal enema: There is no impaction to disimpact, and the anal fissure makes the rectal route actively harmful here
Sequencing trapObtain anorectal manometry: Reserved for constipation that persists despite standard therapy; no therapy has been tried and no alarm sign is present

Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment

when a child's headache needs imaging · migraine vomiting is not a pressure sign · the treatment ladder · drugs that raise pressureIs anything abnormal outside the headache history: the examination, the fundus, the growth chart or the vitals?

Source vignette Pt — 13 yo F, 2 years of similar headaches: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worse with activity, with nausea; now monthly instead of every other month, same characteristics; menarche at 12, periods now regular; this one began after a sleepover, she vomited twice and could not finish her homework; intermittent acetaminophen only · Exam — temperature 37 °C, alert and oriented, pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal, no papilledema described · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned no additional testing, computed tomography (CT) of the head, a urine toxicology screen, serum electrolytes and lumbar puncture
The decision point

This headache is already diagnosable: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worsened by activity, with nausea and vomiting, in an adolescent girl with a two-year history of the same thing. Image only if a feature meets an imaging indication. None of the following three features meets one. Vomiting is a diagnostic criterion of migraine, not a pressure sign. The disability ("could not finish her homework") measures severity, and no guideline images for severity. The increase in frequency is a change in rate, not in character. The headaches "have the same characteristics" and remain monthly. The change tracks the arrival of regular menses since menarche. The examination is normal, including the pupils, and no papilledema is described. No additional testing is needed. Imaging is reserved for an abnormal neurologic examination, signs of raised intracranial pressure, or a dramatic change in headache characteristics.

When papilledema is present, imaging is indicated. Then find why the pressure is high; the medication list often answers it. An adolescent on isotretinoin with a month of morning headache and vomiting, brief blurring of vision, bilateral disc edema and full visual fields has drug-induced intracranial hypertension. A mass at the optic chiasm would cut the fields. Optic neuritis is painful, acute and usually affects one eye.

Defining criteria Indications for neuroimaging in pediatric headache — (1) abnormal neurologic examination findings, such as weakness or ataxia; (2) signs of raised intracranial pressure, such as papilledema; (3) a dramatic change in headache characteristics. None is present here · Not an indication — a modest rise in frequency when the headaches keep the same character, remain relatively infrequent, and have a physiologic explanation for the change · Migraine, diagnostic features — pulsatile, unilateral (may be bilateral in children), hours to days; photophobia and phonophobia; nausea or vomiting; ± aura; normal neurologic examination. Formal criteria add ≥5 prior attacks lasting 2–72 hours in patients under 18 (4–72 in adults); beyond 72 hours is status migrainosus (ICHD-3, International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition)
Pertinent positives & negatives Two years of similar headaches — recurrent and stereotyped; excludes "first and worst," which is the thunderclap gate · Vomited twice — a migraine criterion; it becomes a pressure sign only when it is morning vomiting, projectile, or paired with papilledema · Pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal — closes indication (1) and, in the absence of described disc edema, indication (2) · Menarche at 12, now regular cycles — the physiologic explanation for the change in rate, so the change is explained · Afebrile, alert and oriented — excludes meningitis, so lumbar puncture is not indicated · Began after a sleepover — sleep deprivation is a named migraine trigger, not evidence of ingestion
Classify first: headache in a child
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence for management
Examination and fundus normal?"Pupils equal and reactive... remainder of neurologic examination normal"; no papilledemaCloses both of the first two imaging indications, and the IIH (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) branch with them (in-context: papilledema would be expected)
Character or only rate?"Similar headaches over the past 2 years"; "every other month… now monthly," same featuresRecurrent, not first-and-worst; a rate change only, which does not meet "dramatic change in characteristics"
Explanation for the change?"Menarche at age 12; menstrual periods now regular"A physiologic cause is identified, so the change is accounted for
Systemic signs?"Temperature 37 C," alert, normal vitalsNo infection, no toxidrome
Tier fingerprint done: nothing but intermittent acetaminophen · failed: 2 years of attacks with inadequate abortive dosing and timing, the actual unmet need · bothered: missed schoolwork, which justifies better treatment, not more testing.
Management ladder: headache in a child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Clinical diagnosis; trigger diary (sleep, meals, menses, screens); sleep-hygiene and hydration counseling; no laboratory or imagingAny red-flag gate is breached, or attacks recur despite trigger control
2Abortive therapy at first symptom, at full weight-based dose: ibuprofen or acetaminophen, rest in a dark quiet room, antiemetic if vomiting blocks oral dosingAn early, adequately dosed NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) fails
3Triptan for refractory attacks, then consider daily prevention (propranolol, amitriptyline with cognitive behavioral therapy, topiramate) if attacks are frequent or disablingReassess prevention after a trial of at least 2 months
Exit / de-escalationMedication-overuse headache: withdraw the offending analgesicSimple analgesics on ≥15 days/month, or triptans, or any combination of triptans, analgesics or opioids, on ≥10 days/month, for more than 3 months
Numbers that gate & exit ramps Diagnostic: up to 3 days per attack; ≥5 prior attacks of 2–72 hours. Escalation: frequent or disabling attacks (consider prevention), and the overuse thresholds above. The exam answer versus clinical practice: the exam keys the preventive rung, though a pediatric trial found amitriptyline and topiramate no better than placebo. That trial result does not change the keyed rung. · Papilledema → magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with MR (magnetic resonance) venography, then LP (lumbar puncture) with an opening pressure; a normal MRI with a high opening pressure means intracranial hypertension, idiopathic or drug-induced. · Fever with meningismus → lumbar puncture. A thunderclap headache → noncontrast CT, then LP if negative. · Wakes from sleep, worse on waking or with Valsalva → MRI, however migrainous the rest sounds. · Focal deficit or ataxia → Brain Tumors in a Child. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty → MRI with sellar views; see Brain Tumors in a Child. · Household all symptomatic → carboxyhemoglobin. Image any child who is immunocompromised, shunted, or anticoagulated.
Intracranial hypertension: check the drug list Who — women of childbearing age, obesity or recent weight gain, and drugs: retinoids and vitamin A (isotretinoin for acne), tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline) and growth hormone · Symptoms — daily headache worse lying flat and in the morning, better standing, with nausea and vomiting; transient visual obscurations; pulsatile tinnitus; diplopia from a cranial nerve VI palsy · Signs — bilateral papilledema with enlarged blind spots and full visual fields, otherwise a normal neurologic exam; a lesion at the chiasm would cut the fields (bitemporal hemianopia) · Workup — MRI with MR venography first, to exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis; then LP (lumbar puncture): opening pressure over 250 mm H2O with normal CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) · Treatment — stop the offending drug, which usually resolves it; weight loss; acetazolamide
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination normal, including the fundus? — Yes → the strongest two indications are closed · First and worst, or recurrent and familiar? — Recurrent → no urgent pathway · Did the character change, or only the rate? — Rate only → not a dramatic change · Is there a physiologic explanation for the change? — Menarche and regular cycles → yes · Any systemic signal: fever, altered sensorium, abnormal vitals, growth failure? — None → make a diagnosis and a treatment plan, not a test
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Neurologic exam, fundi and growth chartFirstNormal exam, no papilledema, growth on trackPrimary headache, usually migraine: no testing
None: clinical diagnosis of migraineConfirmsNo test confirms migraineDiagnosis rests on the history and a normal exam
MRI of the brain, for a red flagBy branchMass or hydrocephalusRed flags: focal deficit, papilledema, waking from sleep, change in character
Noncontrast head CTBy branchBlood in a thunderclap headacheSubarachnoid hemorrhage; LP if the CT is negative
MRI of the brain with MR venography, for papilledemaBy branchNormal: no mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosisRaised pressure without a structural cause; proceed to LP
Lumbar puncture with opening pressureBy branchOpening pressure over 250 mm H2O with normal CSF, after a normal MRI and MR venographyIntracranial hypertension, idiopathic or drug-induced; with fever and meningismus, LP for meningitis
CarboxyhemoglobinBy branchElevated, with the household affectedCarbon monoxide exposure
Head CT for recurrent headache, normal examSkipStable character, normal examNo imaging needed; chronic headache that earns imaging gets MRI
Scenario bank
  1. 10 yo M, 1 year of bilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and vomiting, relieved by sleep, normal examination → Reassurance, trigger diary, and early-dose ibuprofen → Pediatric migraine
  2. 13 yo F with 2 years of migraines, now with papilledema and vomiting on waking → MRI of the brain → Suspected intracranial mass
  3. 16 yo F, obese, daily headache with pulsatile tinnitus and papilledema, MRI of the brain normal → Lumbar puncture with opening pressure → Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
  4. 15 yo M, sudden headache maximal within seconds while lifting weights, worst of his life, normal examination → Noncontrast CT of the head → Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage
  5. 4 yo M, 12 h of headache with T 39.2, nuchal rigidity, irritable, no focal deficit or papilledema → Lumbar puncture → Bacterial meningitis
  6. 8 yo F, 6 months of headaches with a normal neurologic examination, height crossed from 50th to 5th percentile with weight held → MRI of the brain with sellar views → Suprasellar mass
  7. 12 yo M with morning headaches and nausea on winter weekdays; mother and brother affected, all better away from home → Carboxyhemoglobin level → Carbon monoxide exposure
  8. 6 yo F, frontal headaches only on school afternoons, squints at the board, normal neurologic examination → Ophthalmologic examination with refraction → Uncorrected refractive error
  9. 13 yo F, 3 years of episodic headaches now monthly and predictable in the 2 days before each period, unchanged in character → Menstrual migraine → Trigger counseling and timed NSAIDs
  10. 15 yo M using ibuprofen or acetaminophen on 20 days per month for a headache that is now daily and dull → Continuing the daily as-needed analgesic → Medication-overuse headache
  11. 16 yo M taking oral isotretinoin for severe acne, with 1 month of daily throbbing frontal headache that is worse in the morning, occasional nausea and vomiting, partial relief from acetaminophen, and brief blurring of the left eye at sports practice; blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg; pupils equal and reactive; bilateral optic disc edema with decreased visual acuity and full visual fields; no meningismus; normal strength, reflexes and sensation → Drug-induced intracranial hypertension → Isotretinoin (a retinoid) impairs CSF resorption; MRI with MR venography, then LP; stop the drug
  12. 15 yo M taking minocycline for acne for 3 months, with daily morning headache and pulsatile tinnitus; bilateral papilledema with full visual fields; MRI of the brain with MR venography is normal; lumbar puncture opening pressure is 340 mm H2O with normal CSF → Discontinue minocycline → Tetracycline-induced intracranial hypertension; it usually resolves off the drug, with acetazolamide added for persistent symptoms
  13. 11 yo M started on growth hormone 4 months ago for growth hormone deficiency, with 3 weeks of headache that is worse lying down and on waking, brief episodes of graying vision, and bilateral papilledema; full visual fields and an otherwise normal neurologic exam → MRI of the brain with MR venography → Exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis before LP; growth hormone-induced intracranial hypertension
Decoy note Awakening from sleep would indicate imaging, and it is absent here. The homework detail measures disability, which sets the treatment tier and never the imaging threshold. The near-doubling of frequency is real but explained.
Pearls A change in frequency needs an explanation; a change in character, an examination finding or a pressure sign needs a scan. · Reassurance is defensible only when you can name the criteria you cleared. · Change in rate ≠ change in character. Ask what changed. If the only change is "more often," look for the physiologic cause (menarche, a new schedule, a new medication) before you look at the brain. · MRI for chronic and progressive; CT for acute and hemorrhagic. The right decision to image still needs the right modality. · Boundary: nocturnal awakening, morning vomiting, and headache worsened by Valsalva are pressure signs even when the rest is textbook migraine. They take precedence over the migraine features. · Migraine onset and changes in frequency cluster around menarche. Through the same estrogen link, menstrual migraine is the commonest cause of headaches that got worse this year in an adolescent.
Pairs with Brain Tumors in a Child covers the same complaint at the same age and sex, on the opposite side of the imaging gate. There, the headache came with papilledema, a height percentile crossing, and Tanner 1. Here it comes with a normal examination and an explained change in frequency. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? Primary Headache in an Adult covers the headache-type differential once imaging has been excluded. Low Back Pain in an Adult uses the same gating logic in a different region. The pain's severity never opens the gate, and a specific finding always does. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin A excess as a cause of pseudotumor cerebri. Ask: is the patient taking a retinoid or a vitamin A supplement? Part I Headache in a School-Age Child covers the whole workup once the gate opens, through the posterior fossa tumor it most often finds. Ask: does the exam show ataxia as well as papilledema?
Transferable rule Findings, not suffering, cross an imaging threshold. The examination, the fundus, the tempo of change in character, and the systemic signs decide imaging. Frequency, duration, and disability decide only the treatment tier. When a pattern changes and you can name why, the change is explained and is not a red flag.
Mirror twinCT scan of the head: Imaging requires examination findings, pressure signs, or a change in character, and none is present; even where imaging is indicated for a chronic pediatric headache, the modality is MRI
Salient decoyUrine toxicology screen: Toxic ingestion presents with altered sensorium, pupillary abnormality, respiratory depression, or seizure; she is alert with reactive pupils, and the sleepover is a sleep-deprivation trigger
Sequencing trapSerum electrolyte measurement: Two episodes in a well-hydrated, alert adolescent change no management decision; the clinical findings already answer the question electrolytes would ask
True-fact-wrong-slotLumbar puncture: She is afebrile with a normal examination, and IIH (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) would show papilledema; lumbar puncture before imaging in a patient with pressure signs is also out of order
Unchecked attributeCluster headache, for the adolescent on isotretinoin: Unilateral periorbital or temporal attacks in men aged 20 to 50, with no papilledema; this headache is daily, frontal, worse in the morning and comes with bilateral disc edema
Salient decoyOptic chiasm glioma: The blurred vision pulls toward the visual pathway, but a chiasm lesion causes bitemporal field loss, and his fields are full
True-fact-wrong-slotOptic neuritis: Disc swelling with blurred vision is real there, but it brings acute vision loss and eye pain, usually in one eye, without morning headache and vomiting
Salient decoyViral encephalitis: Headache and vomiting fit, but encephalitis needs fever and altered mental status; he is afebrile and alert with no meningismus
