Urinary Tract Infection in a Child

assign the tract, then name the risk factor · reflux grade sets treatment and outcomeIs this infection febrile or afebrile, does the bladder empty, and what grade did the cystourethrogram show?

WorkupRisk factorsRefluxPractice
Bottom line

Assign the tract before the cause. The anatomic causes of recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI) in a child, reflux above all, produce recurrent pyelonephritis rather than recurrent cystitis; emptying problems produce lower-tract disease. Afebrile recurrent cystitis in a constipated child is urinary stasis: a loaded rectum compresses the bladder and urethra so it never empties, and the lasting treatment is a long-term laxative.

  • Lower tract (cystitis): dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, afebrile, without flank or back pain.
  • Upper tract (pyelonephritis): fever, flank or back pain, vomiting and an ill appearance; the pattern reflux produces.
  • Reinfection, not relapse: a 6-week symptom-free gap after an adequate short course (3 days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a lower-tract infection) makes relapse unlikely.
  • Vesicoureteral reflux: retrograde urine flow through a congenitally short intravesical ureter.
  • Reflux grade: mild I to II, dilating III to V. Grade I stays in the ureter and II reaches the pelvis without dilation; grade III dilates the ureter and pelvis with little or no blunting, IV obliterates the fornices, and V adds gross dilation and a tortuous ureter.
  • Reflux nephropathy: recurrent febrile infection leaves focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis; enough scarring is chronic kidney disease, which in a child presents as secondary hypertension, proteinuria and failure to thrive.
Workup
Imaging after a febrile UTI First, under age 2 – renal and bladder ultrasound; VCUG only if it shows hydronephrosis, scarring or other signs of high-grade reflux or obstruction, or the course is atypical or complex · First, age 2 or older – no imaging; observe · Recurrent febrile UTI – ultrasound and VCUG at any age, even when the ultrasound is normal again: ultrasound shows dilation and scarring but cannot show reflux · Other VCUG indications – fever of 39 °C or higher with an organism other than Escherichia coli; signs of chronic kidney disease such as poor growth or hypertension · Timing – ultrasound after treatment, to avoid false-positive findings from the acute infection; sooner only if the child is not improving
Recurrent infection: the risk factors
Which tract, then which risk factor
Risk factorThe tellNot it when
Urinary stasis from constipationRecurrent afebrile cystitis in a constipated child, hard stool in the vault, midline anal fissuresFever or flank pain
Dysfunctional voidingHolds urine all day, holding maneuvers, soft stoolsConstipation explains the emptying
Vesicoureteral refluxRecurrent febrile infection or pyelonephritis in an infant; hydronephrosis on ultrasoundAfebrile, suprapubic, no flank pain
Posterior urethral valvesMale infant, weak stream, palpable bladder, bilateral hydronephrosisFemale, normal stream, no distended bladder
Primary immunodeficiencySevere, multi-site infections, pyelonephritis rather than cystitis, failure to thriveSimple cystitis only; history otherwise unremarkable
Sexual abuseGenital injury or bleeding, behavioral change, disclosure; real but rareNormal genitalia; fissures explained by constipation
Inadequate treatmentNever resolved, or recurrence within days of finishing; same organism6-week symptom-free gap after an adequate course
Reflux: the grade sets the plan
Read the grade off the VCUG Ultrasound – shows hydronephrosis; mild there describes the dilation, not the reflux · VCUG – shows ureteral filling with or without a dilated collecting system, and is what assigns the grade · Mild – ureter or pelvis without dilation: usually resolves, a change believed to stem from the intravesical ureter lengthening with growth · Dilating – dilated ureter and pelvis, often blunted calices: less likely to resolve, more likely to recur and scar · Secondary – a boy with hydronephrosis and a weak stream has outlet obstruction causing the reflux, a different pathway
Management ladder: primary reflux
TierInterventionEscalate when
Mild (I to II)Observation, with or without prophylactic antibiotics (the rules below decide); expect spontaneous resolutionA breakthrough febrile UTI
Dilating (III to V)Prophylactic antibiotics (recommended under 1 year, and with bladder-bowel dysfunction while it is present and being treated; may be considered over 1 year with prior UTI and no dysfunction), with surgery as the next optionFebrile breakthrough on prophylaxis: consider ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic bulking injection
Established scarringAnnual blood pressure, height, weight and urine protein through adolescenceHypertension, proteinuria or declining function: chronic kidney disease care
Who gets continuous prophylaxis: American Urological Association (AUA) Under 1 year, after a febrile UTI – recommended, at any grade · Under 1 year, found by screening – recommended for grades III to V; may be offered for I to II · Bladder-bowel dysfunction – recommended while it is present and being treated; treat the dysfunction, preferably before any surgery, at every grade · Over 1 year, with prior UTI, no dysfunction – may be considered · The trial – in the Randomized Intervention for Children with Vesicoureteral Reflux (RIVUR) trial (age 2 to 72 months, grades I to IV, after a first or second symptomatic UTI), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis halved recurrent UTIs, with no significant difference in renal scarring
Practice
  1. 4-year-old girl has her third afebrile cystitis this year functional constipation since day care suprapubic tenderness, no back pain hard stool in the rectal vault Last episode 6 weeks ago, after 3 days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole T 37.2 °C · normal genitalia → Urinary stasis → afebrile, suprapubic and no back pain is the lower tract, so the cause is incomplete emptying: a loaded rectum compresses the bladder and urethra, and ascending Escherichia coli colonizes the residual urine. Reflux produces recurrent upper-tract, febrile disease, and a child with reflux would likely have had at least one febrile episode by now. Three days is an adequate course for a lower-tract infection, and a 6-week symptom-free gap means reinfection, not relapse
  2. 6-month-old girl was treated for her first febrile urinary tract infection ultrasound: hydronephrosis cystourethrogram: dilated ureter with blunting of the calices Feeding well; growing along the 50th percentile Afebrile · blood pressure (BP) 88/54 mm Hg → Prophylactic antibiotics → under 1 year with reflux and a febrile infection, continuous prophylaxis is recommended at any grade, and dilating reflux is less likely to resolve and more likely to recur and scar, so observation alone is not an option. Surgery is the next rung, considered after a febrile breakthrough infection on prophylaxis, not immediately
  3. 22-month-old girl had afebrile cystitis 3 months ago soft daily stools then 2 days of fever to 39 °C and irritability; vomited once, now drinking well right costovertebral angle tenderness afebrile within 48 hours of oral cefixime · culture: Escherichia coli → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → fever, vomiting and flank tenderness put this infection in the upper tract, and once treated, a first febrile urinary tract infection (UTI) under age 2 gets a renal and bladder ultrasound. Soft daily stools leave nothing for a laxative to treat, and reassurance with a repeat culture ignores the febrile imaging rule
  4. 4-year-old girl with recurrent cystitis has hard stools every 5 days hard stool fills the rectal vault post-void residual urine is increased No fever with any episode; no back pain Afebrile · rectal tone normal → The dilated rectum compresses the bladder and urethra, preventing complete voiding → residual urine is colonized by organisms ascending from the perineum. Reflux of urine to the kidney is the upper-tract, febrile mechanism, which this afebrile child lacks, and the organism ascends from the perineum rather than crossing the bowel wall
  5. 6-month-old boy had his first febrile urinary tract infection afebrile within 48 hours of oral cefixime Ultrasound after treatment: bilateral hydronephrosis normal urinary stream T 37.1 °C now · catheter culture: 100,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli → Voiding cystourethrogram → after a first febrile infection under age 2, an abnormal renal and bladder ultrasound (hydronephrosis, scarring, or findings of high-grade reflux or obstruction) is the indication for a voiding cystourethrogram, which shows and grades the reflux. No further imaging fits only a normal ultrasound, and prophylaxis waits for the cystourethrogram result
  6. 5-year-old girl has dysuria and frequency for 2 days bruising of the labia small amount of vaginal bleeding normal rectal examination; soft stools Mother noticed blood on her underwear yesterday Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase, nitrite → Evaluate for sexual abuse and involve child protective services → genital injury or bleeding is the tell of sexual abuse, a real cause of urinary infection in children though rare: evaluate and involve child protective services. A normal rectal examination with soft stools leaves no constipation for a laxative, and an afebrile infection needs no voiding cystourethrogram
  7. 6-month-old boy had his first febrile urinary tract infection reflux left untreated cystourethrogram: dilated ureter with blunted calices Mother reports no recurrence; examination normal T 37.0 °C · BP 90/56 mm Hg → Focal interstitial fibrosis from recurrent parenchymal infection → blunted calices place him in the dilating group, which scars: recurrent febrile infection puts bacteria in the parenchyma, and inflammation and ischemia leave focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis, which in enough quantity is chronic kidney disease. Glomerular inflammation follows group A streptococcal skin or throat infection, and acquired renal cysts belong to children on dialysis; a quiet interval and a normal examination do not rule out future scarring
  8. 4-year-old girl is seen after treatment of her third cystitis this year hard stools every 4 days since starting day care hard stool in the rectal vault Symptom free now; normal genitalia Afebrile · urine culture after treatment not sent → Long-term laxative therapy → treat the risk factor: a long-term laxative softens stools, stops the withholding and lets the dilated rectum shrink, which relieves the bladder; treating the infection alone guarantees another episode. Prophylaxis belongs to reflux, which this lower-tract pattern does not suggest, and an afebrile infection needs no voiding cystourethrogram
  9. 3-year-old boy given daily prophylaxis since grade IV reflux was diagnosed at 8 months now his second febrile infection on prophylaxis left flank tenderness T 39.0 °C · urine culture: Escherichia coli → Surgical correction of the reflux → a febrile breakthrough infection on prophylaxis means prophylaxis has failed: consider open ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic injection of a bulking agent, with curative intent. The guideline names changing the agent as an option after a single febrile breakthrough with no renal cortical abnormalities; this is his second, and removing the kidney is not among the curative interventions the guideline names
  10. 18-month-old girl had 2 days of fever to 39.2 °C and irritability first urinary tract infection afebrile within 24 hours of oral cefixime ultrasound after treatment is normal catheter urinalysis: leukocyte esterase, nitrite, pyuria · culture: 80,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli → No further imaging → a first febrile infection under age 2 gets a renal and bladder ultrasound, and a voiding cystourethrogram only if it is abnormal or a febrile infection recurs. Prophylaxis waits for the cystourethrogram result, so neither distractor applies yet. A fever of 39.2 °C with Escherichia coli does not meet the other-organism indication
  11. 6-year-old boy with reflux has had three Proteus urinary infections intermittent flank pain for 2 months branching staghorn calculus on imaging Urine pH 8.5; no family history of stones Afebrile · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL → A struvite stone from urease-producing bacteria → an alkaline pH above 8 with Proteus means urease, and urease-producing organisms make struvite. Reflux makes calcium stones through stasis, but recurrent Proteus points to urease. Reflux never makes uric acid stones, which come from overproduction, as in tumor lysis
  12. 5-year-old girl has her fourth cystitis in a year soft daily stools holds her urine all day at school crosses her legs and squats on her heel when urgent Afebrile · normal rectal examination → Timed voiding with behavioral therapy → holding urine all day with holding maneuvers is an emptying problem of the bladder itself, and emptying problems cause lower-tract disease: timed voiding with behavioral therapy (voiding habits are part of prevention). Soft daily stools leave nothing for a laxative to treat, and an afebrile infection needs no voiding cystourethrogram
  13. 2-month-old boy has his second febrile urinary tract infection weak urinary stream palpable bladder above the pubis Uncircumcised; feeding less than usual for 2 days Afebrile on intravenous antibiotics · ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis → Voiding cystourethrogram → a male infant with a weak stream, a palpable bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis has outlet obstruction until shown otherwise: the voiding cystourethrogram shows the dilated posterior urethra. Ultrasound shows dilation but cannot show reflux or confirm valves, and circumcision can lower the infection risk but does not relieve an outlet obstruction
  14. 3-year-old boy has had two episodes of pyelonephritis pneumonia three times two skin abscesses drained weight has fallen from the 50th to the 5th percentile T 38.2 °C · normal stream → Primary immunodeficiency → severe infections (pyelonephritis rather than cystitis) at several sites with failure to thrive mean defective clearance across sites and organisms. Constipation-driven stasis gives simple cystitis in one tract, and reflux explains febrile kidney infections but not pneumonia, abscesses or poor growth
  15. 5-year-old girl whose grade II reflux was diagnosed at age 2 hard stools every 4 days daytime wetting most days Taking daily antibiotic prophylaxis; no infection this year Afebrile · urinalysis normal today → Treat the bladder and bowel dysfunction → bladder-bowel dysfunction is screened and treated alongside reflux at every grade, preferably before any surgery, and prophylaxis is recommended while the dysfunction is present and being treated. Surgery, if needed, preferably comes after that treatment, and the guideline ties a change in therapy to a symptomatic breakthrough infection, which she has not had
  16. 3-year-old girl was started on oral cefdinir for a febrile urinary tract infection 72 hours ago left flank tenderness drinking; not vomiting Culture: Escherichia coli susceptible to cefdinir T 39.4 °C → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → no improvement by 48 to 72 hours on a drug the organism is susceptible to means looking for an abscess or obstruction: renal and bladder ultrasound, a repeat culture, intravenous antibiotics and admission. Switching drugs answers a resistant organism, and this one is susceptible; a voiding cystourethrogram does not look for an abscess
  17. 7-year-old boy has dilating reflux treated since infancy renal scarring on imaging no infection in 2 years Height at the 25th percentile; parents ask what to check at each visit BP 104/66 mm Hg · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL → Blood pressure and urinalysis for proteinuria → established scarring can progress to chronic kidney disease, which in a child shows as secondary hypertension, proteinuria and failure to thrive: blood pressure, urine protein and growth, checked yearly. An ultrasound alone does not show those, and uric acid has no role in reflux
  18. 4-year-old girl has her third cystitis this year untreated constipation with hard stools each episode cleared with a short antibiotic course Symptom free between episodes Afebrile · hard stool in the rectal vault → Lengthening the antibiotic course → the risk factor is mechanical, and a short course is adequate for a lower-tract infection, so a longer course treats the episode, not the disease. A laxative, and fiber with water, both target the constipation that keeps the bladder from emptying
  19. 8-month-old boy had a febrile urinary tract infection last month cystourethrogram: grade IV reflux weak, dribbling urinary stream palpable bladder Straining to void; urine dribbles between feeds Afebrile · BP 94/58 mm Hg · creatinine 0.6 mg/dL → Evaluate for bladder outlet obstruction → a boy with a weak stream and a palpable bladder has outlet obstruction causing secondary reflux, a different pathway: here the reflux is the consequence, not the disease, so look for posterior urethral valves on urethral views. Prophylaxis alone or a ureteral reimplantation leaves the obstruction in place
  20. 8-year-old girl has had febrile urinary tract infections since infancy headaches proteinuria small, scarred kidneys on ultrasound; no cysts Takes no medications; no recent sore throat or rash BP 128/84 mm Hg · height below the 5th percentile → Reflux nephropathy with chronic kidney disease → recurrent febrile infection scars the interstitium in wedges, and widespread scarring presents as secondary hypertension, proteinuria and failure to thrive, the endpoint prophylaxis prevents. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis follows group A streptococcal skin or throat infection and injures the glomerulus; the kidneys here are small and scarred, with no cysts
  21. 4-year-old boy has his second febrile urinary tract infection, fever to 39.1 °C First at 13 months; ultrasound then normal right costovertebral angle tenderness afebrile within 24 hours of antibiotics repeat renal and bladder ultrasound normal urine culture: Escherichia coli → Voiding cystourethrogram → a second febrile infection needs a voiding cystourethrogram at any age, even when the ultrasound is normal again, because ultrasound cannot show reflux. No further management is right only for a first febrile infection, and daily prophylaxis waits for the cystourethrogram result, since reflux is not yet known
  22. 2-year-old girl had reflux into the ureter only at 6 months no infections since repeat cystourethrogram now shows no reflux No surgery or injection was done Afebrile · BP 92/58 mm Hg → The intravesical ureter lengthens as the child grows → mild reflux often resolves on its own, a change believed to stem from the intravesical ureter lengthening as the child matures; remodeling of the junction and maturing bladder function may contribute alongside it, but the defect is the short tunnel
Reading the urine Specimen – catheter if not toilet trained, clean catch if trained · Leukocyte esterase – from lysed neutrophils; marks pyuria (more than 5 white cells per high-power field) · Nitrite – nitrate reductase of Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and Proteus; a negative result does not exclude a UTI, especially with frequent voiding in infants · pH above 8 – urease; think Proteus mirabilis · Culture – 100,000 CFU/mL or more by clean catch, 50,000 or more by catheter, of one uropathogen · Hematuria alone – not a UTI · Pyuria without bacteriuria in an adolescent – nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea
Febrile UTI: treat before the culture returns Empiric – after the urinalysis, chosen by local sensitivity patterns and adjusted to the culture: oral options include cefixime, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole · Route – oral is preferred, pyelonephritis included; intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone for age under 2 months, vomiting, an unstable or ill child, or failure of oral therapy · Blood tests – complete blood count, blood culture and procalcitonin only if ill-appearing, unvaccinated or under 2 months · No better by 48 to 72 hours – resistant: switch to a susceptible drug; susceptible: ultrasound for abscess or obstruction, repeat culture, intravenous antibiotics and admission · After a good response – no routine repeat culture · Prevention – treat constipation, prophylaxis for reflux per the AUA rules, voiding habits, front-to-back wiping
The constipated child Constipation is the commonest modifiable risk factor for recurrent cystitis in a young child, and the mechanism is purely mechanical. Functional constipation that dates to day-care entry is the stressor-driven withholding trigger. Hard stool with normal rectal tone argues against both a neurologic cause and anal trauma. Midline anal fissures are a complication of chronic constipation; alongside normal genitalia, they argue against injury, while a fissure off the midline may have another cause, such as Crohn disease. Treating the infection without the constipation treats the episode, not the disease; the maintenance laxative runs for at least 2 months, and the dilated rectum narrows on treatment.
Scarring and stones Reflux scarring is tubulointerstitial: bacteria in the parenchyma cause inflammation and ischemia, which lead to wedge-shaped fibrosis, and the glomeruli are lost secondarily. Only the grade predicts the long-term outcome, and the course if untreated follows the severity in this patient: never carry a severity adjective from one study to another. Reflux makes calcium stones through stasis and struvite stones through urease-producing organisms.
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the obstructive counterpart, with the same cystourethrogram and hydronephrosis but reflux secondary to outlet obstruction; is there a weak stream or a palpable bladder, and is the reflux the disease or its consequence? Part II Pyelonephritis: oral versus intravenous route in adults. Part I Constipation in a Child: the upstream cycle whose urinary complication this is. Transferable rule

A disease name strongly associated with a complaint comes to mind before the finding that discriminates it, and recently learned associations come fastest. Convert each into a question: here, which tract is infected, and what grade did the cystourethrogram show?
